This paper formulates a corresponding bulk-transport problem for many birds. We construct an explicit directed corridor network in a Poisson disk forest and impose a common temporal headway at its waypoints. The maximum current equals a minimum vertex-cut capacity and is achieved by repeated flight along vertex-disjoint paths. The same schedule maximizes completed traversals at every finite horizon, with constant forward speed and no internal waiting. For a forest belt of fixed depth, exact transverse superadditivity yields an almost-sure deterministic current-density limit. A uniform shape theorem for an asymmetric planar dual identifies the current when depth and width grow together. For diverging depth bounded by a constant times width, this current equals the width-first, depth-second limit and is independent of the positive aspect ratio. When diagonal corridors are available, bulk current is positive at sufficiently low obstacle intensity and zero at sufficiently high intensity. For stochastic demand, an upstream admission queue is stable at every rate below the finite-network capacity.

Abstract: We explore how synchronization in coupled oscillator networks may be employed to perform a variety of computing tasks. These systems are becoming more attractive as an alternative to conventional digital computers due to the increasing energy demands of the latter, particularly for large-scale problems in machine learning and artificial intelligence. The ubiquity of coupled oscillator networks means that oscillator-based computing can be thought of as a universal computing paradigm encompassing systems with a diversity of physical realizations, e.g. as analog circuits, neurological systems, spintronic systems. The bridge between the dynamics of coupled oscillator networks and computational primitives they implement is the Ising model, which originates in statistical physics, and when applied to oscillator networks, explains the emergence of globally complex and disordered synchronization patterns from local interactions in the network. We discuss the application of coupled oscillator networks to three fundamental computing operations. First, oscillator networks as specialized hardware solvers of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems, with the solution encoded in the synchrony patterns. Second, oscillator networks as associative memory systems, enabling storage and retrieval of data represented through phases of oscillations. Finally, oscillator networks as a dynamical implementation of attention, with synchronization providing the mechanism for the alignment of keys to queries. The ability of oscillator networks to implement these computational primitives paves the way for novel realizations of intelligent systems through a variety of physical substrates.

</details>

Abstract: Central Pattern Generators (CPGs) have long inspired the design of rhythms that combine endogenous generation and exogenous interaction. In neurodynamics and engineering studies, CPGs have been primarily analysed and designed as networks of coupled oscillators. In contrast, the present article regards CPGs as networks that propagate events through excitable rather than oscillatory nodes. The proposed event-based perspective reduces the design of network-level rhythmic properties to the tuning of local nodal input-output characteristics. This reduction enables a distributed and robust design methodology: nodes can be tuned independently, they can be heterogeneous, and the global rhythm results from local event propagation rather than from a specific global tuning of the network parameters. The present article builds on previously introduced concepts that parallel existing characterizations of oscillators: the event describing function (eDF), which characterises the propagation delay of a node, and the event phase response curve (ePRC), which characterises the phase sensitivity of a node. Event-based CPGs made of excitable rather than oscillatory nodes emerge as a principled design framework for robust rhythm generation.

</details>

Abstract: Europe's future power system will rely heavily on wind and solar power and must remain resilient during prolonged periods of low wind and solar generation, known as variable renewable energy (VRE) droughts. To capture such rare events, adequacy assessments increasingly draw on decades of weather data, but the conversion of weather into power is largely treated as fixed. It remains unclear which modelling choices in this conversion matter for representing these droughts, and whether they matter as much as the weather itself. Here we systematically compare these choices side by side (bias correction, wind speed extrapolation, capacity layouts, turbine and photovoltaic configurations, and wake losses) and trace their effects through VRE droughts to the design of a net-zero European power system, using 85 years of reanalysis data. We find that modelling choices barely change how often VRE droughts occur or when the system is stressed. They do, however, determine how much capacity is needed to withstand that stress. By altering the electricity delivered during droughts, they shift required capacity by up to 480 GW, which is comparable to the spread across the most critical weather years. Modelling exercises should therefore use multiple weather years; bias-correct and regionally validate weather inputs; explicitly represent resource heterogeneity, forward-looking technologies, and wake losses; and judge these choices by their effect on the low-generation tail, not only on the mean.

</details>

Abstract: In this article, we present socx, a GPU-accelerated solver for lifted convex reformulations of linear stochastic optimal control under chance constraints, implemented in JAX. We demonstrate that by exploiting the sparse and independent structure of the problem, distributed optimization can reduce it to simpler problems: independent linear-quadratic tracking (LQT) problems and Euclidean projections onto sets. These simpler problems can be solved in parallel and then coupled using the constraints. To validate our solver, we run it on a hover-linearized 3D quadrotor and show a speed-up of up to $98\times$ over MOSEK and up to $2224\times$ over SCS. socx also solves horizons up to $N=1120$, whereas MOSEK runs out of memory at $N=320$. We present ablations to isolate the key components that enable the speed-up.

Abstract: Sampling-based reachability estimates reachable sets from finitely many simulated trajectory endpoints. Existing guarantees often control missed probability mass or approximation error relative to the convex hull of the reachable set, leaving the geometric error relative to the reachable set incompletely characterized. We study this error as a problem of support estimation under flow distortion. Our assumptions combine a uniform lower bound on the local volume density of the initial set, a lower bound on the sampling density, and a one-sided Lipschitz constant $μ$ for the vector field. These conditions admit initial sets with corners and dynamics that may expand or contract. In the fine-accuracy regime, $\tilde{\mathcal O}\bigl(2^ne^{nμT}(R/r)^n/(ρκ)\bigr)$ independent endpoint samples suffice for Hausdorff accuracy $r$ using the endpoint cloud. Here, $n$ is the state dimension, $T$ is the horizon, $R$ is the volume-equivalent radius, and $ρ$ and $κ$ quantify sampling density and local volume density. For $n\ge2$ and sufficiently small $κ$, a minimax lower bound over all estimators based only on independent endpoints matches these dependencies up to a dimension-dependent factor $2\cdot4^n$ and logarithmic factors, within the stated parameter range and when the state domain accommodates the construction. The exponential burden in dimension, and in the horizon for expanding systems, is therefore intrinsic to this observation model. Planar experiments illustrate the predicted effects of corners and contraction; robot-arm experiments show how empirical accuracy deteriorates with dimension.

</details>

In this model a rate parameter multiplies the complete right-hand side of the excitation equation, forcing term included. The input resistor of the excitation integrator sets that parameter, so no state, delay element, or controller is added. Sampled waveforms were recorded at two resistor values, with two independent runs each. The measured excitation excursion agrees with numerical integration to within three percent at the baseline setting and five percent at the rate-controlled setting. Between the two settings the excitation excursion contracts by a factor of thirteen. At the rate-controlled setting the recovery excursion exceeds prediction by a factor of eight. This excess traces to a displaced operating point on the state-dependent recovery rate. Thermal drift in the multiplier chain and leakage at the high-impedance recovery-rate divider could each produce it, and the present data do not separate them. A tested bipolar input stage strongly loads that divider, a constraint absent from the ideal equations. The divider, not the sub-hertz signal bandwidth, sets the amplifier input-stage requirement.

Abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) hedges data-driven two-stage stochastic programs against error in the distribution estimated from a finite record, and standard ambiguity sets differ in how they treat realizations absent from that record. A divergence ball around the empirical distribution contains only reweightings of the record, whereas a transport ball also contains distributions supported off the record, including on realizations the data-generating process cannot produce, against which the decision is then hedged as well. We instead propose a Kullback-Leibler (KL) ball centered at a density model fitted to the record, the learned nominal, which lets the adversary up-weight costly unobserved realizations in proportion to the probability the model assigns them. Solving the resulting problem poses a second difficulty, because it can accommodate only a few scenarios, and an independent sample of that size is likely to omit the rare realizations on which the worst case concentrates. We therefore build the scenario set adaptively, alternating between solving the finite problem and drawing new realizations from the learned nominal, steered toward the worst case at the current decision, with importance weights that correct the draws back to the model. On a multi-item newsvendor problem and a capacity expansion problem on realistic grid data, centering the ball at the learned nominal rather than at the record lowers cost under distribution shift, at comparable in-distribution cost, when the record is scarce and the model class captures structure that lets it extrapolate beyond the record. The advantage fades as the record grows or as the shift departs from the structure the model has learned.

</details>

Abstract: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is widely used for image-guided radiotherapy, but reducing the number of projections to lower dose and scan time makes reconstruction increasingly ill-posed. We present EUReCA (End-to-end Unified REconstruction across Clinical Acquisitions), a geometry-aware feed-forward model for variable-view clinical linac CBCT. For a given acquisition trajectory, EUReCA accepts 8-100 projections with a single set of weights, without view-count-specific retraining; the same architecture and training recipe extend unchanged to other clinical trajectories. It combines learned projection features with an in-frame Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstruction. The model encodes each projection with a shared multiscale backbone, back-projects features into multiresolution 3D grids using the acquisition geometry, aggregates variable numbers of views at fixed computational cost, and refines the volume with a global 3D transformer and multilevel decoder. On simulated data, EUReCA achieved 29.9-33.2 dB PSNR with 10-100 views and outperformed all applicable feed-forward baselines; it also exceeded iterative optimization-based methods while running orders of magnitude faster. On 15 measured patient CBCT scans evaluated against vendor reconstructions, EUReCA achieved the best performance at every tested view count. These results suggest that geometry-aware, measurement-anchored feed-forward reconstruction can provide a practical and flexible foundation for variable-view linac CBCT.

</details>

Abstract: Radiomics extracts quantitative features describing tumor shape, intensity, and texture from medical images to build models that predict clinical outcomes. However, large feature sets increase the risk of overfitting in small datasets, and building an end-to-end workflow often requires programming expertise. We present MEDiml (Medical Image Analysis with Machine Learning), open-source radiomics software available as a Python package (MEDiml-pkg) and a no-code desktop application (MEDiml-app). Both run on the same computational engine, and code generation exports graphically configured workflows as executable Python code. Feature extraction follows the Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI) standards. MEDiml is built around complexity minimization: features are grouped into levels of increasing complexity (morphological, intensity, textural,l and filter-based), a model is trained at each level, and the simplest level not significantly outperformed by more complex ones is retained. Applied to five oncological datasets (2,104 scans), MEDiml achieved AUCs of 0.65 to 0.82, with morphological or intensity features sufficient in four of the five tasks. Resources: www.mediml.app.

Abstract: Myocardial Infarction (MI) is a severe and potentially fatal cardiac condition caused by myocardial injury due to ischemia, and timely detection can substantially reduce its mortality. Electrocardiography (ECG) is the primary diagnostic modality for MI, but manual interpretation is susceptible to human error. Finally, we apply LIME, Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients to verify that the image models attend to the ECG waveform rather than the background. These results indicate that careful signal normalization combined with ML and DL models can support fast and accurate automated MI screening.

Abstract: Functional MRI (fMRI) is widely used to characterize brain activity and connectivity, but conventional gradient-echo echo-planar imaging produces high acoustic sound-pressure levels by operating gradient hardware near its limits. Scanner noise can increase anxiety and motion, particularly in noise-sensitive populations, and can evoke auditory responses that confound both task-based and resting-state measurements. Looping Star (LS) is a near-silent, T2*-weighted acquisition that uses slowly varying gradients and multiplexed, temporally staggered coherences. Conventional LS rotates planar encoding trajectories across shots to achieve three-dimensional coverage. Because these planes intersect near the center of k-space, sampling is dense at low spatial frequencies but sparse and nonuniform at the periphery, limiting efficiency when relatively few shots are combined for high temporal resolution. We introduce Looping Kooshball (LKB), a complementary LS trajectory that extends through all three spatial dimensions within each shot. LKB is designed to improve volumetric k-space coverage while preserving the echo-formation and coherence-crushing properties of LS. We compare LKB with conventional LS using point-spread-function analysis, in-bore acoustic measurements, structural phantom imaging, and preliminary visual-motor fMRI experiments. We evaluate whether LKB reduces undersampling artifacts and improves temporal stability and functional-activation detection without sacrificing the near-silent operation of LS.

</details>

The method alternates two steps: a flow matching model first learns the distribution of the acquired data; then, the sample and the background are jointly estimated by minimising a Kullback-Leibler divergence between observed and simulated distributions via regularised proximal gradient steps. Abstract: First-derivative edge detectors such as Sobel, Prewitt, Roberts and Scharr measure absolute grey-level differences. We revisit the log-gradient magnitude, a relative-gradient edge operator, and motivate it by analogy with the superderivative, a multiplicative derivative in which the independent variable is perturbed multiplicatively rather than additively. In one and two dimensions the logarithm of the superderivative is a radial logarithmic derivative; its local, origin-free, isotropic analogue is the magnitude of the logarithmic gradient. The resulting operator measures relative rather than absolute change, giving an edge-strength map that is invariant under global intensity rescaling. We present the theory, show how the operator can be implemented in two steps---a classical gradient kernel plus a pointwise division---and compare it with standard first-derivative filters on synthetic images with ground-truth edges and on the official BSDS500 benchmark. We also study a parametric family that interpolates between the absolute gradient and the log-gradient; empirically, the best members are small intermediate exponents, which edge the classical kernels by a small but statistically detectable margin in the per-image metric and, with the same Gaussian smoothing as the single-$σ$ Canny, match it in ODS and lead it in OIS and AP, while the tuned Canny remains ahead in ODS. The single-threshold margin over the kernels does not replicate on the held-out test split, and the fully relative endpoint is never the best member, its ranking depending on the edge-map normalisation. The contribution is the construction and the invariance it buys, not a new state of the art.

</details>

Abstract: Generative reconstruction can recover high-quality images from undersampled acquisitions, but state-of-the-art generative priors commonly rely on iterative sampling. Reducing the number of iterations lowers inference cost but also removes opportunities for progressive distributional refinement, making it difficult to retain image realism without sacrificing reconstruction fidelity. Drift modeling offers an alternative by shifting progressive refinement to training, thereby enabling one-step sampling without an iterative inference trajectory. Existing drifting methods, however, do not account for the imaging operator when modeling distributional drift. We propose DriftRecon, a generative method for one-step medical image reconstruction that performs drifting directly in the nullspace of the imaging operator. DriftRecon uses nullspace-restricted noise to construct training samples and a multiscale generator that incorporates measurement conditioning across resolution levels, with its generated component projected onto the operator nullspace. To control the fidelity--realism trade-off at inference, a conditional guidance parameter continuously steers the same generator between measurement-conditioned and unconditional generation. We derive a guidance-dependent similarity-kernel temperature schedule that preserves the guidance-weighted mass receiving strengthened supervision, thereby progressively localizing drift interactions as guidance increases to limit the associated loss of reconstruction fidelity. Experiments in sparse-view CT and accelerated MRI reconstruction show that DriftRecon outperforms established generative reconstruction methods and recent drifting models while producing reconstructions in a single forward pass.

</details>

Abstract: Real-time magnetic resonance imaging of the vocal tract makes speech articulation directly observable, but the trade-off between temporal resolution and signal quality introduces substantial noise and obscures fine articulatory detail. Since clean references cannot be acquired for a moving vocal tract, supervised denoising approaches are not applicable in this setting. We propose a self-supervised denoising framework that combines spatiotemporal super-resolution learning with pseudo-supervision derived from a variance-stabilized non-local means filter. A dual-model fusion strategy balances noise suppression and preservation of high-frequency articulatory structure. Experiments on the USC-75 multi-speaker dataset under natural noise conditions show that the ensemble raises the signal-to-noise ratio by 11.9 dB on unseen subjects while attaining more high-frequency articulatory content in the frames. Among tuned implementations of anisotropic diffusion, block-matching filtering, non-local means and pre-smoothed non-local means, every configuration that achieves comparable noise suppression does so at the cost of high-frequency content or of structural fidelity. Under severe added Gaussian, Rayleigh and Rician noise, peak signal-to-noise ratio improves by 7.6 to 11.8 dB and structural similarity roughly triples. An ablation shows that the variance-stabilized pseudo-supervision is an essential element for denoising, and that the effect is attributable to the hard thresholding contained in the stabilization transform.
